content: Sucralfate can reduce the absorption and effectiveness of digoxin when both are administered orally. This occurs due to inhibition of gastrointestinal (GI) absorption. It is recommended to avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. If co-administration is necessary, measure serum digoxin concentrations before starting sucralfate and monitor levels closely. Adjust the digoxin dose by approximately 20% to 40% as needed. Sucralfate decreases the absorption and effectiveness of dolutegravir by binding to cations in the GI tract. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. If dolutegravir must be used, administer it at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after sucralfate or other medications containing polyvalent cations. Sucralfate reduces the absorption of bictegravir by cation binding in the GI tract. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is required. Bictegravir can be taken on an empty stomach 2 hours before antacids containing aluminum, magnesium, or calcium. Simultaneous administration or taking bictegravir within 2 hours after such antacids is not recommended. Sucralfate significantly reduces the absorption of ciprofloxacin due to chelation within the GI tract. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs. To minimize this interaction, ciprofloxacin should be taken 2 hours before or 6 hours after sucralfate. Use caution and monitor closely. Sucralfate decreases the absorption of delafloxacin by binding to cations in the GI tract. Oral delafloxacin forms chelates with alkaline earth and transition metal cations. Administer delafloxacin at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after sucralfate. Therapy modification and close monitoring are advised. Sucralfate reduces the absorption of fleroxacin, gemifloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, and ofloxacin by inhibiting GI absorption. These interactions apply only to the oral forms of both agents. Use caution and monitor closely. To minimize interactions, these antibiotics should be taken 2 hours before or 6 hours after sucralfate. Sucralfate decreases the absorption of ketoconazole and levoketoconazole by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs. Use caution and monitor closely. Sucralfate reduces the absorption of tetracycline-class antibiotics, including doxycycline, minocycline, oxytetracycline, and demeclocycline, by inhibiting GI absorption. These interactions apply only to the oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown, but caution is advised. Sucralfate decreases the absorption of phenytoin, fosphenytoin, and ethosuximide by inhibiting GI absorption. These interactions apply only to the oral forms of both drugs. The clinical significance is unknown, but close monitoring is recommended. Sucralfate reduces the absorption of lansoprazole by inhibiting GI absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both drugs. Separate the administration of lansoprazole and sucralfate by at least 30 minutes. Magnesium sulfate and potassium chloride increase the toxicity of sucralfate. Co-administration with medications that cause fluid and electrolyte abnormalities may increase the risk of seizures, arrhythmias, and renal impairment. Use caution and monitor closely. Sodium sulfate, potassium sulfate, and magnesium sulfate also increase the toxicity of sucralfate. The same precautions apply as with magnesium sulfate and potassium chloride. Vitamin D analogs may increase the absorption of aluminum from sucralfate, potentially leading to aluminum toxicity. Avoid co-administration of sucralfate and vitamin D. Use caution and monitor closely. Sucralfate increases the levels of aluminum hydroxide due to pharmacodynamic synergy, resulting in additive aluminum content. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. Sucralfate may cause constipation, diarrhea, dizziness, dry mouth, flatulence, headache, indigestion, insomnia, nausea, vertigo, vomiting, bezoar formation, gastrointestinal discomfort, hypersensitivity reactions, and hyperglycemia. Use caution in patients with diabetes, as hyperglycemia has been reported. Sucralfate is minimally absorbed and acts locally at the site of ulcers. It does not alter the recurrence or severity of duodenal ulceration after healing. Avoid taking antacids within 30 minutes of a sucralfate dose. Aluminum absorption from sucralfate is increased, so use caution in patients with chronic renal failure or those undergoing dialysis. Fatal complications, including pulmonary and cerebral emboli, have been reported with inappropriate intravenous administration of oral suspension. Administer oral suspension only via the oral route. Sucralfate is classified as pregnancy category B. It is likely safe during lactation, as it is minimally absorbed and unlikely to be excreted in breast milk. Controlled studies in pregnant women show no evidence of fetal risk.
